passage: From my bench by the park gate I watched two children argue over the one swing. The girl called Indu said to Suraj, "You push me, then I push you." Suraj frowned and looked at the swing, then nodded. Indu climbed on and he pushed. She counted out loud to ten. They swapped: Suraj sat and Indu pushed, counting to ten again, a little louder. Neither looked cross at the end. I could not tell whether Suraj really liked the deal, but he stayed and played until the light went.

qa.q: How high did Indu count on each turn?
qa.a: Indu counted out loud to ten.

qa.q: What might Suraj be feeling when he frowns and looks at the swing before nodding?
qa.a: He may be unsure at first, weighing the offer, and then accept it as fair. The narrator cannot know for certain.

qa.q: What other approach could work if Suraj had said no, and why?
qa.a: They could ask a grown-up nearby to set a fair turn for each. An adult can settle it when two children cannot agree.

qa.q: How does the exchange look to the narrator on the bench?
qa.a: The narrator sees two children sort it out fairly on their own. The narrator also admits not knowing how Suraj really felt.

grounding: A child proposes taking turns pushing, and both children get a fair, counted turn on the swing.

passage: The slide line stretched past the tap. Shankar ran along the side, squeezed in between two children near the front and grabbed the ladder. "Hey!" shouted a girl. "Back of the line!" shouted the others. Shankar slid down with a big grin that faded when he looked round. Chaitanya, who had been waving Shankar over to stand with him at the back, folded his arms. At the next break Chaitanya walked past Shankar without a word, and Shankar stood by the wall alone.

qa.q: Where did Shankar squeeze in?
qa.a: Shankar squeezed in between two children near the front of the line.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling when his grin faded as he looked round?
qa.a: Shankar felt uneasy and a little ashamed. He got his turn, but he saw everyone was angry.

qa.q: What could Shankar have done instead, and why?
qa.a: Shankar could have gone to Chaitanya at the back and waited, or asked someone, "Can I go after you?" Shankar would get a turn and keep Chaitanya's goodwill.

qa.q: How does the pushing in look to Chaitanya?
qa.a: Chaitanya had waved Shankar over to wait together, so it feels like someone Shankar was invited to wait with chose to skip everyone. That hurts, so turning away makes sense. 😔

grounding: A child pushes to the front of the slide line, gets a turn and loses another child's goodwill.

passage: By the school slide, "Come on, join the line," said Karthik. "It's too long," said Jagdish. "There are ten kids." "It moves fast." "I don't want to play anyway." "You said you wanted the slide all morning." "It's a baby game." Jagdish kicked a stone toward the corner. "I'm going to sit there." Karthik shrugged and joined the line. He went down twice. From the corner Jagdish picked at the wall and said to nobody, "It's boring."

qa.q: Where did Jagdish go instead of joining the line?
qa.a: Jagdish went to sit in the corner.

qa.q: What might Jagdish really be feeling when he says, "I don't want to play anyway"?
qa.a: Jagdish may be disappointed and tired of the long line, and covering it up by acting as if nothing matters. Watching from the corner and calling it boring hint at that.

qa.q: What could Jagdish try instead, and why?
qa.a: Jagdish could ask Karthik to save a place, or count the children and wait. Waiting gets the slide that was wanted all morning.

qa.q: How does the moment look to Karthik?
qa.a: Karthik offered help and sees Jagdish walk away from the slide that was wanted all morning. Karthik may be puzzled and shrug it off.

grounding: A child walks away from a long slide line saying the game does not matter, which protects feelings but gets no turn.

passage: In the colony park, Yusuf ran to the swing and shouted, "My turn!" Hafsa held the chains tighter and swung higher. Yusuf shouted louder and got only a shrug, so he kicked the pole and went home. The next day he stood by the swing for a while, then tried something different. "Can I go after you?" "Okay," said Hafsa. "Ten more swings." Yusuf sat on the bench and counted along with her. When his turn came, he swung hard and grinned. On Friday he asked the same way again.

qa.q: What did Yusuf ask Hafsa the next day?
qa.a: Yusuf asked, "Can I go after you?"

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling when he kicked the pole and went home?
qa.a: Yusuf felt frustrated and cross, because shouting had got him nowhere.

qa.q: What other approach could Yusuf add, and why?
qa.a: He could offer a trade, like "I push you, then you push me." A trade gives Hafsa something too, so it is easier for Hafsa to say yes.

qa.q: How do the two ways of asking look to Hafsa?
qa.a: Shouting sounds like a demand, so holding on tighter is natural. Asking politely leaves the choice with Hafsa, so Hafsa agrees and sets the count.

grounding: A child whose shouting failed asks politely the next day and keeps polite asking as the new plan.

passage: Rain drummed on the roof of the crèche, and only a few minutes were left before the parents came. Pankaj wanted Ishita's doll in the yellow dress, and Ishita wanted the red toy truck in Pankaj's hands. Pankaj held the truck out. "You have the truck, I have the doll, then we swap back." Ishita paused, then nodded and put the doll in his arms. Ishita drove the truck under the table with engine noises while Pankaj brushed the doll's hair. When the bell rang for pick-up, they swapped back without being told.

qa.q: What did Pankaj offer to swap for the doll?
qa.a: Pankaj offered the red toy truck.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling about the doll before he made his offer?
qa.a: Pankaj wanted a turn with the doll and was hopeful about getting one. The truck was his way of asking for it.

qa.q: What other approach could work if Ishita had said no, and why?
qa.a: They could ask a grown-up for a timer so each gets a turn with each toy. A timer gives a fair count neither has to argue over.

qa.q: How does the swap look to Ishita?
qa.a: Ishita gets the truck that was wanted, so the trade feels fair. Swapping back when the bell rang shows Ishita trusted it.

grounding: A child swaps a toy truck for a turn with the other child's doll so both get something wanted.

passage: Only ten minutes of play were left before the school bus, and Aarav had a box of cars that Irfan badly wanted. Irfan clutched the big truck to his chest. His brother Pradeep, sitting beside him, asked only, "Are you going to play?" Irfan whispered to himself, "If I share the truck, then Aarav shares his cars." He took a breath and pushed the truck across the mat. "You can drive it." Aarav slid the box over. "Take the red one." They raced them until the bell.

qa.q: What did Irfan whisper to himself?
qa.a: Irfan whispered, "If I share the truck, then Aarav shares his cars."

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling as he clutched the truck to his chest?
qa.a: Irfan felt reluctant and a little worried about letting the truck go. Clutching it and taking a breath show it.

qa.q: What could Irfan try if Aarav did not share back, and why?
qa.a: He could ask a grown-up to help them set turns with a timer. A timer treats both children the same way.

qa.q: How does the offer look to Aarav?
qa.a: Aarav gets to drive the big truck and passes over the box in return. Both children feel the trade is fair.

grounding: A child reasons that sharing the truck will bring a share of the other child's cars, which makes handing it over less costly.

passage: On Monday, Maria and Devika pulled on the same wooden train until Maria shouted, "Teacher!" The teacher came, took a sand timer from the shelf and said, "One turn each, until the sand runs out." On Tuesday Maria had the train first and watched the sand fall, her hands behind her back. On Friday Devika reached for the train, and Maria fetched the timer herself and turned it over.

qa.q: What did the teacher propose for the turns?
qa.a: The teacher proposed a sand timer, with one turn each until the sand runs out.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling as she watched the sand fall with her hands behind her back?
qa.a: Maria was probably impatient but trying hard to wait. Keeping her hands behind her back shows she is holding herself to the rule.

qa.q: What other approach could Maria and Devika use without a teacher, and why?
qa.a: They could agree, "You go first, then me," and count together. A plan they make themselves works even when no adult is near.

qa.q: How does the timer look to Devika?
qa.a: Devika knows a turn is coming and cannot be pulled away halfway. That makes it easier to trust the plan.

grounding: Two children pull on one toy until the teacher is asked, and a sand timer sets the turns, which the child follows.

passage: "Can I hold your robot?" asked Francis's little brother Thomas. "No!" Francis pulled it behind his back. "Why not?" "It'll get used up." "Toys don't get used up." "Yes they do. If you touch it, it turns into a different robot. A worse one." "That's silly." "It isn't!" Francis ran to the bedroom and pushed the robot under his pillow. Thomas stood in the doorway. "Then can we play trains?" "Not till the robot is safe." Thomas walked away and lined up the trains alone.

qa.q: Where did Francis put the robot?
qa.a: Francis pushed the robot under his pillow.

qa.q: What was Francis afraid of when he said the robot would be used up?
qa.a: Francis was afraid the robot would turn into a worse one if Thomas touched it. The fear is not real, but it decided what Francis did.

qa.q: What small step could help Francis, and why?
qa.a: Francis could let Thomas hold the robot for a minute while Francis watches. Seeing it stay the same would show the fear is not true.

qa.q: How does the moment look to Thomas?
qa.a: Thomas is left out and confused, because the reason makes no sense. Thomas ends up lining up the trains alone.

grounding: A child fears a toy will be used up or changed once his brother touches it and hides it, so the fear decides the play.

passage: Note from the art teacher, Friday. Kashish had a tray of paints that several children wanted. A boy in a red shirt held out a crayon and said, "You can use this. Can I use your paints?" Kashish smiled and slid the tray over. Chetan had been watching from the end of the table. He picked up his green crayon, walked round and held it out. "You can use this. Can I use your paints?" Kashish smiled again and made room. I said nothing and just watched. Mr Ali

qa.q: What did Chetan hold out to Kashish?
qa.a: Chetan held out his green crayon.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling while he watched from the end of the table?
qa.a: Chetan was eager and probably a little unsure how to ask. He learned by watching the boy in the red shirt first.

qa.q: What could Chetan try if Kashish had said no, and why?
qa.a: He could ask another child, or wait for a turn. A second plan means one no does not end it.

qa.q: How does the offer look to Kashish?
qa.a: Kashish gets something back, so sharing feels fair. Smiling twice shows the trade is welcome.

grounding: A child copies another child who trades a crayon for a turn with the paints, and it works.

passage: On Monday, Salma clutched her toy giraffe while Hansa asked to hold it, and would not let go. On Tuesday she said, "Let's play shop. I am the shopkeeper and you are the customer. You borrow the giraffe and bring it back at closing time." She nodded to herself. "Customers always bring things back." Hansa borrowed it and gave it back when Salma rang the bell. On Thursday Hansa asked again, and Salma said, "Come to my shop," and handed the giraffe over at once.

qa.q: When was the giraffe to be brought back?
qa.a: The giraffe was to be brought back at closing time.

qa.q: What was Salma feeling on Monday when she clutched the giraffe and would not let go?
qa.a: Salma was worried about losing the giraffe or having it changed. Holding on tight shows she did not feel safe giving it up.

qa.q: What other approach could help Salma feel safe sharing, and why?
qa.a: She could ask a grown-up to set a timer for each turn. A timer promises the giraffe comes back.

qa.q: How does the game look to Hansa?
qa.a: Hansa is a customer who gets a turn with the giraffe and hands it back at closing. It is play, so Hansa gives it back happily.

grounding: A child turns sharing into a shop game where the other child borrows the toy and returns it at closing time.
